studies.title: Single dose creatine improves cognitive performance and induces changes in cerebral high energy phosphates during sleep deprivation.

says: Pooled reviews (meta-analyses) and clinical trials show creatine improves certain cognitive measures like memory and processing speed (Studies 1, 2, 8).
But effects on other cognitive domains remain mixed or statistically non-significant across different groups (Studies 2, 3, 9).
Creatine improved memory with a standard average difference of 0.29 (likely range, 0.04 to 0.53) (Study 1).
Who was studied: healthy adults, older adults, and sleep-deprived people tested in clinical trials (Studies 1, 2, 12).
Creatine can also improve intelligence and reasoning in healthy people (Study 3).

parts.assessment: Creatine supplement use improves certain cognitive measures like memory and processing speed (Study 2).

evidence: A systematic review found that creatine supplement use improved overall measures of memory compared with placebo (Study 1).
Subgroup (a smaller group picked out of the whole) analyses revealed a significant improvement in memory specifically in older adults aged 66 to 76 years (Study 1).
Another pooled review (meta-analysis) noted positive effects on memory, attention time, and processing speed time (Study 2).
A trial with 123 people showed a small helpful effect of creatine on cognitive tasks (Study 9).
Single-dose creatine studies showed reduced cognitive deterioration during sleep deprivation (Study 12).
breakdown.effect_size: Creatine improved memory with a standard average difference of 0.29 (likely range, 0.04 to 0.53) (Study 1).
breakdown.applies_to: Healthy adults, older adults, and sleep-deprived people tested in clinical trials (Studies 1, 2, 12).
breakdown.strength: Multiple systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials support mild cognitive benefits, especially in older or stressed adults (Studies 1, 2, 8).

concluded.said: Creatine supplementation enhanced measures of memory performance in healthy individuals, especially in older adults (66-76 years).

Current evidence suggests that creatine monohydrate supplementation may confer beneficial effects on cognitive function in adults, particularly in the domains of memory, attention time, and information processing speed. Larger robust clinical trials are warranted to further validate these findings.

Oral creatine administration may improve short-term memory and intelligence/reasoning of healthy individuals but its effect on other cognitive domains remains unclear. Findings suggest potential benefit for aging and stressed individuals. Since creatine is safe, future studies should include larger sample sizes. It is imperative that creatine should be tested on patients with dementias or cognitive impairment.

CrM supplementation with and without exercise and diet intervention may help middle-aged and older adults maintain muscle mass and strength while favourably affecting selected markers of health and cognitive function. Individual cognitive and biomarker findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

Our study, in combination with the literature, implies that creatine might have a small beneficial effect. Larger studies are needed to confirm or rule out this effect. Given the safety and broad availability of creatine, this is well worth investigating; a small effect could have large benefits when scaled over time and over many people.

Our findings suggest that this supplementation protocol may be a promising, safe, effective, and practical dietary strategy for improving clinical outcomes and elevating brain creatine concentrations in perimenopausal and menopausal women.

Our results show that a dose of 0.2 g/kg creatine is associated with a reduced deterioration in cognitive performance during sleep deprivation. Although the effect is less pronounced than with a high dose of 0.35 g/kg, there is still an improvement of up to 12%.

Creatine supplementation improved physical (strength endurance) and prolonged cognitive (Stroop accuracy) performance, yet it did not combat MF-induced impairments in short sport-specific psychomotor or cognitive (Flanker) performance.

Our results show that creatine induces changes in PCr/Pi, ATP, tCr/tNAA, prevents a drop in pH level, and improves cognitive performance and processing speed. These outcomes suggest that a high single dose of creatine can partially reverse metabolic alterations and fatigue-related cognitive deterioration.

rows.search_query: (fish oil OR omega-3) AND blood pressure
rows.tldr: Fish oil lowers blood pressure a little in people with high blood pressure, and hardly at all in others.
rows.explanation: Pooled trials found fish oil lowers blood pressure by a few points (Studies 1, 3). The drop was larger in people who already had high blood pressure (Studies 2, 5), and small in healthy volunteers (Study 4).
rows.still_open: Whether the small drop lasts beyond a year, and what dose matters.
